title: runtime/scheduler: refine short/long classification using rolling EWMA of observed prefill time (with safeguards)
author: Omar El-Sayed
release_notes: Internal-only: improves mixed-workload classifier accuracy by incorporating rolling EWMA of observed prefill time; guarded by feature flag and conservative fallbacks.
description:
Context: As part of the mixed-workload scheduler prototype, we currently classify requests as SHORT vs LONG using prompt-length thresholds (and a stubbed prefill predictor). In trace replays we’ve seen misclassification in two common cases: (1) same token length but very different prefill time due to model/hardware/kernel selection, (2) long-context requests that occasionally land in a faster prefill regime (cache effects / smaller effective attention) and get over-penalized.

This PR adds a rolling EWMA estimator of observed prefill time and uses it to refine the short/long split on a per-route/per-model basis, while keeping the prompt-length threshold as the safe default. The estimator is intentionally conservative and comes with multiple safeguards to avoid oscillations, bad cold-start behavior, or classifier “churn” during bursty traffic.

What changed (high level): Add a PrefillEWMAEstimator fed by per-request observed prefill duration (prefill-only, not decode). The estimator outputs a predicted prefill_ms for the *next* request keyed by (model_id, route_id, gpu_sku). Classification uses: if EWMA is healthy -> compare predicted prefill_ms against long_prefill_ms_threshold; else -> fall back to prompt_tokens_threshold (existing behavior). We also clamp and gate updates to reduce impact from outliers.

Key behavior details: (1) Cold start: EWMA is disabled until min_samples is reached (default 50) OR the request rate exceeds a “warm” threshold (to avoid waiting forever in low-volume routes). (2) Outlier handling: updates are skipped if prefill_ms exceeds max_prefill_ms_cap or is below min_prefill_ms_floor; additionally we apply a winsorization clamp to [p05, p95] once we have enough samples to compute approximate bounds (cheap streaming approx). (3) Stability: EWMA alpha defaults to 0.08; we also apply a deadband so that small changes in predicted prefill don’t flip classification around the threshold. (4) Safety kill-switch: if we detect sustained mismatch between predicted prefill and observed prefill (MAPE > 35% over N=200 samples), we disable EWMA for that key for 10 minutes and revert to token-threshold classification. (5) Metrics: new per-classifier metrics to see how often we use EWMA vs fallback, and how often we trip the safety disable.

Why EWMA (vs SRPT-ish predicted cost): We only need a robust binary split for the two-queue scheduler. EWMA gives us an inexpensive, low-variance signal that captures real runtime/hardware behavior without introducing a more complex predictor that is harder to reason about during canary.

Implementation notes: We feed observed prefill time from existing tracing spans added in scheduler instrumentation (enqueue->first_token already had prefill/decode split in the runtime timeline); this PR adds a small helper that extracts prefill duration reliably even when streaming begins late due to batching.

Config / flags: Behind runtime.scheduler.mixed_workload_classifier.use_prefill_ewma (default: false). All thresholds are in config with conservative defaults. If the flag is off, behavior is identical to today.

Testing: Added unit tests for estimator gating (min_samples), clamping/outlier skip, deadband behavior, safety disable + re-enable, and deterministic classification given a synthetic timeline. Added a small simulation test that replays a synthetic mix where prompt tokens is a weak predictor but prefill ms is stable; classifier should converge to correct split within ~200 samples.

Perf: No measurable overhead in microbench; estimator update is O(1) and on a hot path but guarded by a cheap sampling (default 1/20 requests) for feeding metrics + EWMA updates. In replay benchmarks (A100, llama-70b-ish workload mix) we saw classifier mismatch rate drop from ~18% -> ~7% and p95 tail improve an additional 4–6% on top of the two-queue scheduler, with throughput within noise (+/-1%).

Rollout: Keep default-off. For perf-canary, we can enable EWMA only for a single route/model tuple and monitor: (a) ewma_enabled_ratio, (b) ewma_safety_disable_total, (c) short_queue_wait_p95, (d) long_queue_starvation_guardrail.

Snippet (core logic):

classifier.go: predicted := ewma.Predict(key) if ewma.Healthy(key) && abs(predicted-last_predicted) > deadband_ms { if predicted >= long_prefill_ms_threshold => LONG else SHORT } else { // fallback token threshold }

Related: ENG-4822 (classification), ENG-4831 (fairness guardrails), PR #8439 (starvation guardrails), PR #8444 (instrumentation).
commits: runtime/scheduler: add PrefillEWMAEstimator and keying by (model, route, sku)
runtime/metrics: export ewma health + fallback counters and mismatch gauge
runtime/scheduler: integrate EWMA prediction into short/long classifier with deadband + safeguards
tests: unit tests for ewma gating/clamping/safety-disable + simulation replay
docs: config comments + operator notes for perf-canary enablement
conversation:
Sofia Ivanova (review): I like the direction, but I’m worried we’ll end up flipping class on every small movement around the threshold. Can we add a deadband or hysteresis? Also want a hard fallback to prompt tokens for low-sample keys.

Omar El-Sayed (author): Added deadband_ms (default 3.0ms) and a min_samples gate (default 50). If not healthy, classifier uses the existing prompt token threshold path.

Lena Fischer (review): Two questions: (1) are we updating EWMA per request? (2) any risk of “learning” a slow prefill regime due to a transient kernel regression and then biasing classification for a long time?

Omar El-Sayed (author): (1) Updates are sampled 1/20 by default; classification reads are always O(1). (2) Added safety disable: if predicted vs observed MAPE > 35% for 200 samples, disable EWMA for 10m and fall back. Also EWMA alpha is 0.08 so it adapts but doesn’t lock-in forever.

Grace Kim (review): Please confirm we’re measuring prefill only. Some traces show first token time includes queueing and batching delay.

Omar El-Sayed (author): Yep—this PR extracts prefill duration from the internal runtime timeline events (prefill_start/prefill_end). If those aren’t present (older builds), we mark the observation invalid and skip EWMA updates.

Yuki Sato (review): Keying includes gpu_sku, good. Do we also need kernel profile / quantization profile in the key? Otherwise we might mix regimes.

Omar El-Sayed (author): Good call. I tried adding quant_profile but it exploded cardinality in one test route. For now: key includes model_id + route_id + gpu_sku; if quant profile becomes a common cause of regime mixing, we can add it behind a separate option. Also added a cardinality cap and eviction policy (LRU) at 2k keys per process.

Julian Moore (review): Metrics naming bikeshed: prefer runtime_scheduler_classifier_* prefix to match dashboards. Also can we include a counter for ewma_safety_disabled_total?

Omar El-Sayed (author): Renamed metrics to runtime_scheduler_classifier_ewma_enabled_ratio, runtime_scheduler_classifier_fallback_total{reason=...}, runtime_scheduler_classifier_ewma_safety_disable_total, and runtime_scheduler_classifier_predicted_prefill_ms (sampled histogram).

Jonas Weber (review): Can you attach a quick before/after on the trace replay suite and confirm throughput deltas are within our mixed-workload standard bounds?

Omar El-Sayed (author): Attached results in the PR description summary: mismatch 18%->7%, incremental p95 improvement 4–6% on top of two-queue; throughput +/-1% (within bounds). Also ran on L4: benefit smaller (~2% p95) but no regression.

CI note: initial sim-tests run failed due to a flaky time-based assertion; updated to deterministic fake clock. Re-run green.

Sofia Ivanova (final): LGTM with the deadband + safety disable. Please keep default-off and make sure perf-canary enables this only in a tight scope.

Merge: Squash merged by Omar El-Sayed after approvals from Sofia Ivanova, Lena Fischer, Grace Kim, and Jonas Weber.
